mainTopic: How the court values damage: the source and method of valuing as one part of sixty, and whether this applies to damage done by a person's own body
overview: The amud opens by closing an earlier question with תיקו, leaving it unresolved. It then asks for the source of the משנה's rule that crop damage is valued as part of a larger field. רב מתנה learns it from ״וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״, and after two challenges the גמרא concludes that the phrase teaches two things: there is no liability for eating in רשות הרבים, and the damage is valued against another field. Three אמוראים agree that the eaten part is valued as one part of an area sixty times larger, though they differ on the unit. A ברייתא about a 'small garden bed' is read the same way. Another ברייתא rules out valuing with a קב or a בית כור. רב פפא's explanation of it is rejected, and the final reading is that a damaged קב is valued neither by itself nor inside a huge field, but as one part of sixty. In a real case, רב נחמן applied the sixty rule to a man who cut down a date palm. רבא objects that the rule was taught for damage by one's property, not by one's own body. אביי then shows that the ברייתא רבא seems to rely on proves nothing, since an animal-damage ברייתא is just as silent about sixty.

steps.title: Closing the earlier question: it stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its earlier question: should the owner have watched over his animal while it was inside? No answer is found, so the question is left as תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or do we say he should have guarded it there inside? Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a question it started before this section. It ends with תיקו, which means no answer was found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last side of the question is that the owner could have watched the animal right where it was, so he may still be responsible. Since neither side can be proven, the question is left open. When a question ends in תיקו, the outcome is left unsettled.

keyTerms.meaning: To guard it, to watch over it
Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

steps.confusionAlert: תיקו does not mean the owner is exempt or liable. It only means the גמרא could not decide the question.

phrases.english: Or should he have guarded it there inside?
Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a question from earlier on the daf
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question of whether the owner had to guard the animal in place is left unresolved.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה and asking for its source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule on how payment for damage is valued. It then asks where in the תורה this rule comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'How does it pay for what it damaged? etc.' Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the משנה's method for valuing damage. It then asks for the source, setting up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the court values the damaged patch as part of a larger area, a בית סאה. It does not value the small patch on its own. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches this way of valuing.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these things?

phrases.english: How does it pay
for what it damaged, etc.
From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that teaches valuing the damage as part of a larger field

steps.title: רב מתנה brings a פסוק as the source
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנה learns from the words ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ that the court values the damage against a larger field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מתנה said: The פסוק says 'and it feeds in another field.' This teaches that the court values the damage relative to another field.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מתנה answers the question by quoting a פסוק. He reads 'another field' as a guide for how to value the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads ״שָׂדֶה אַחֵר״ as 'a different, bigger field.' So the damaged patch is valued as part of a larger area. It is not valued as a small patch by itself. This matches the משנה's method of using a בית סאה.

keyTerms.meaning: And it feeds in another field (שמות 22:4)
They value, they make an estimate

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic method for valuing crop damage, and the rest of the sugya builds on it.

phrases.english: Rav Mattana said: As the verse says:
"And it feeds in another field" –
this teaches that the court values the damage
relative to another field.
phrases.notes: He means the damaged patch is valued as part of a bigger field, not by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר″ teaches that the damage is valued relative to a larger field

steps.title: The פסוק seems to be needed for a different lesson
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ is already needed to teach something else: there is no liability in רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this phrase 'and it feeds in another's field' is needed to exclude the public domain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב מתנה. It says his פסוק is already used for a different lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase can be read as 'another person's field.' Read that way, it teaches that the owner is liable only for damage in someone's private field, not in רשות הרבים. If the words are used for that lesson, they cannot also be the source for רב מתנה's valuation rule.

phrases.english: But this phrase "and it feeds in another's field"
is needed to exclude the public domain!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי ״וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְאַפּוֹקֵי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב מתנה's source from step 3
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מתנה's use of ״וּבִעֵר בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ as the source for the valuation rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק is already used to exclude רשות הרבים, so it seems it cannot also teach how to value the damage

steps.title: The unusual wording carries an extra lesson
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the תורה could have used simpler wording to teach the רשות הרבים exemption. The exact phrase ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ adds the lesson about valuing against another field.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the verse only meant to exclude רשות הרבים, the תורה could have written ״בִּשְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ״ or ״שְׂדֵה אַחֵר״. Why did it write ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״? To teach that we value the damage against another field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 4. It shows that the phrase can teach both the exemption in רשות הרבים and the valuation rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge said the phrase was already used up for the רשות הרבים exemption. The answer is that a simpler wording would have been enough for that. The particular wording the תורה chose shows that a second lesson is also hidden here.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the תורה or ה׳ as its author

phrases.english: If so, let the Merciful One write
"and it feeds in his fellow's field,"
or alternatively "another field"!
What is meant by "in another field"?
That we value the damage relative to another field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4 by showing that the particular wording points to an extra lesson.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording: a simpler phrase would have been enough for the first lesson, so the chosen phrase teaches a second one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ is fully used up teaching the exemption in רשות הרבים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The particular wording teaches both the exemption and valuing against another field.

steps.title: Maybe the phrase teaches only the valuation rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: perhaps the whole phrase is for valuing the damage. If so, where would the רשות הרבים exemption come from?
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead that the whole phrase comes to teach the valuation rule. Then where do we learn that there is no liability in רשות הרבים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now pushes from the other side. Maybe the phrase teaches only the valuation rule and nothing about רשות הרבים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 showed the phrase is not used up by the רשות הרבים lesson. This challenge asks the reverse question. It suggests the phrase might be used up by the valuation lesson, which would leave the exemption in רשות הרבים with no source.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole phrase

phrases.english: But say that all of it
comes for this purpose;
then to exclude the public domain, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 5 from the opposite direction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 5 that ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ teaches both lessons.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the whole phrase teaches valuation, then the exemption in רשות הרבים has no source.

steps.title: Where the phrase is placed proves both lessons
steps.stepSummary: If the phrase taught only valuation, it would have been written in the verse about payment. Since it appears in the verse about the eating, it teaches both lessons.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the phrase were only about valuation, the תורה should have put it in the payment part of the verse: ״מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״. Why is it written next to ״וּבִעֵר״, the eating? Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 6 by pointing to where in the verse the phrase appears. It concludes that the phrase teaches two lessons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A valuation rule belongs with the payment words. Instead, the phrase is attached to the description of the eating, which tells us where the damage happened. That placement teaches the exemption in רשות הרבים, and the wording itself (from step 5) teaches the valuation rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Next to, in the context of

steps.whatToRemember: ״בִּשְׂדֵה אַחֵר״ teaches two things: there is no liability for eating in רשות הרבים, and damage is valued against a larger field.

phrases.english: If so, let the Merciful One write it
in the context of payment:
"The best of his field and the best of his vineyard
phrases.notes: See שמות 22:4. The גמרא is imagining how the payment words would read with the phrase added.

phrases.english: he shall pay in another field"!
Why do I need that the Merciful One wrote it
next to "and it feeds"?
Learn two things from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתְּבֵיהּ רַחֲמָנָא גַּבֵּי תַשְׁלוּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 and closes the discussion of the source.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Placement in the verse: the phrase sits with the eating, not with the payment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase might teach only the valuation rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Its placement teaches the exemption in רשות הרבים, and its wording teaches the valuation rule.

steps.title: How exactly is the damage valued?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the practical method of valuing the damage against another field.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we value it?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the source is settled, the גמרא asks a practical question. It is setting up the opinions in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing that we value against a larger field is not enough. We still need to know the size of the eaten area and the size of the larger field it is compared to.

phrases.english: How do we value it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where the rule comes from to how the rule is carried out.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The size of the area that was eaten and the size of the larger field used for comparison.

steps.title: Three views on the ratio of sixty
steps.stepSummary: All three אמוראים compare the eaten area to an area sixty times larger. They disagree about the size of the basic unit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא says: a סאה measured within sixty סאין. רבי ינאי says: a תרקב within sixty תרקבים. חזקיה says: a single stalk within sixty stalks.
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים answer the question of how to value the damage. Each gives a different unit, but all of them use the number sixty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that the eaten area is valued as one part of a field sixty times its size. The argument is only about the unit being measured: a large area (a סאה of planting area), half that (a תרקב), or a single stalk.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure; here, the area needed to plant a סאה of seed
Half the planting area of a סאה

steps.whatToRemember: The court values the eaten part as one sixtieth of a larger field. The opinions differ only on the unit: סאה, תרקב, or a stalk.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
A se'a within sixty se'in.
phrases.notes: He means an area big enough to plant a סאה of seed, compared to an area sixty times as big.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai said:
A tarkav within sixty tarkavim.
Chizkiya said:
A stalk within sixty stalks.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא: סְאָה בְּשִׁשִּׁים סְאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8 with three opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The eaten area is valued as one sixtieth of a larger field. The unit is a סאה, a תרקב, or a single stalk, depending on the opinion.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to value the small patch by itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא saying a small eaten area is valued as a small garden bed, which sounds like it is priced by itself and not as part of sixty.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: If the animal ate a קב or two קבין of produce, we do not say 'pay what that produce is worth.' Rather, we look at it as if it were a small garden bed and assess it. Doesn't that mean we value that small bed by itself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that seems to argue with all three אמוראים from the last step. They said to compare the eaten part to an area sixty times bigger, but this ברייתא seems to value the small patch on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא agrees we do not just pay for the eaten produce. But it says to view the eaten spot as a 'small garden bed,' which sounds like pricing that little bed as a separate sale. That would contradict the sixty-times method everyone agreed on in step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from a ברייתא)
A measure of volume (here, the amount of produce eaten)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If it ate a kav or two kavs,
we do not say: pay their value,
rather, we view it
as if it were a small garden bed,
and we assess it.
What, is it not that we assess it by itself?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sixty-times valuation method that all three אמוראים agreed on in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The shared view of the אמוראים that the eaten area is valued as part of an area sixty times larger.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא speaks of viewing the eaten spot as a small garden bed, which suggests valuing it alone, not as one part of sixty.

steps.title: The ברייתא also means valuing against sixty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא also means the small bed is valued as one part of an area sixty times larger.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means we assess it as part of sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in one short line. The 'small garden bed' is not priced alone; it is priced as one part of an area sixty times bigger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only told us not to pay for the bare produce and to think of the spot as land. It did not say how big the comparison area is. So it fits with the אמוראים: the small bed is valued within sixty.

keyTerms.meaning: In sixty: as one part of an area sixty times larger

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees: the damage is valued as a small part of an area sixty times larger, not by itself.

phrases.english: No, it means within sixty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 by reading the ברייתא differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא meant to value the small garden bed by itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means to value the small bed as part of an area sixty times larger, matching the אמוראים.

steps.title: A ברייתא: do not value using a קב or a כור
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא says the valuation should not use a בית קב, because that is 'improving' him, and not a בית כור, because that is 'hurting' him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: We do not assess using a קב, because that improves his position, and not using a בית כור, because that hurts his position.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about what size area to use when valuing the damage. It is short and unclear, so it sets up the next question: what does it mean?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא rules out two sizes: a small one (קב) and a large one (כור). But it does not say who is helped or hurt, or what the area is being compared to. The next steps will explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: An area of land large enough to plant a כור of seed (a big field)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
We do not appraise a kav, because that improves his position,
phrases.notes: 'His' is unclear here; רב פפא will explain who is meant.

phrases.english: and not a beit kor, because that hurts his position.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing the sixty-times method, the גמרא brings a ברייתא about which unit size to use.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Valuation should not be done with a קב-sized area or a כור-sized area, since one helps and one hurts the party involved.

steps.title: What is the ברייתא saying?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the unclear ברייתא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for an explanation of the short ברייתא. It is setting up רב פפא's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא does not say what the קב or כור is being compared to, or whose position is improved or hurt. The גמרא wants these details filled in.

phrases.english: What is it saying?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the ברייתא quoted in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the ברייתא is comparing, and whom it helps or hurts.

steps.title: רב פפא: a קב in sixty helps the מזיק, a כור in sixty hurts him
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains: do not value a קב as part of sixty קבין, since that helps the מזיק, and do not value a כור as part of sixty כורין, since that hurts the מזיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said, this is what it means: We do not appraise a קב within sixty קבין, because that helps the one who did the damage. And we do not appraise a כור within sixty כורין, because that hurts the one who did the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא fills in the missing details of the ברייתא. Both cases use the sixty-times method, and the 'him' is the מזיק, the owner of the animal who must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each size gives an unfair price. Sixty קבין is a plot that sells cheaply, so the damage would come out too low and the מזיק would gain. Sixty כורין is a huge field that sells at a high price, so the damage would come out too high and the מזיק would lose.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who caused the damage (who must pay)

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not cancelling the sixty-times rule. It is only ruling out unit sizes that would make the price unfair to one side.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said, this is what it is saying:
We do not appraise a kav within sixty kavs,
because that benefits the one who caused damage,
and not a kor within sixty kors,
because that hurts the one who caused damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13 by explaining the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא refers to valuing within sixty: a קב in sixty קבין helps the מזיק, and a כור in sixty כורין hurts the מזיק, so neither unit is used.

steps.title: רב הונא בר מנוח objects to רב פפא's reading
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח says רב פפא's reading does not fit the ברייתא's words, because the ברייתא says 'בית כור' and not just 'כור'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח objects: Look at the words 'and not a בית כור'! If רב פפא were right, the ברייתא should have just said 'and not a כור'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בר מנוח attacks רב פפא's explanation from Step 14 by pointing to an exact word in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא read the ברייתא as talking about the damaged spot itself being a כור, valued as part of sixty כורין. But the ברייתא says 'בית כור', meaning 'an area of a כור'. That word suggests a big field that the small damaged spot sits inside, so רב פפא's reading does not match the wording.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it; he raises a strong challenge
A large field area, big enough to plant a כּוֹר of seed

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Manoach objects to it:
This wording, "and not a beit kor"?!
phrases.notes: He is quoting the ברייתא from Step 12. The word to watch is 'בית', which means 'area of'.

phrases.english: It should have said "and not a kor"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's explanation given in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's reading of the ברייתא (a כור valued as part of sixty כורין).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's word 'בית כור' does not fit a reading where the damaged spot itself is a כור. Under that reading it should have said simply 'כור'.

steps.title: A new reading: not by itself, not inside a huge field, but one part of sixty
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח, quoting רב אחא בריה דרב איקא, explains that a damaged קב is not valued alone, and not as part of a whole בית כור, but as one part of sixty.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב הונא בר מנוח said in the name of רב אחא son of רב איקא: This is what the ברייתא teaches. We do not value a קב by itself, because that helps the injured person too much. And we do not value a קב as part of a בית כור, because that hurts the injured person. Rather, we value it as one part of sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רב פפא's reading was rejected, the גמרא gives a new way to read the ברייתא that fits the word 'בית כור'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both cases are about the same small damaged spot, a קב. Valuing it by itself gives a high price and is too generous to the ניזק. Valuing it inside a huge בית כור makes it almost worthless and is unfair to the ניזק. The middle path is valuing it as one part of an area sixty times bigger.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what the source is teaching
The injured party, whose property was damaged

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different reading, not the same idea from another angle. רב פפא said the problem was the size of the unit (a קב in sixty קבין, a כור in sixty כורין). Here the damaged spot is always a קב, and the question is what it is compared to: nothing, a whole בית כור, or sixty times its size.
steps.whatToRemember: A small damaged spot is valued neither alone nor inside a giant field, but as one part of an area sixty times larger.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Huna bar Manoach said

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא,
phrases.english: in the name of Rav Acha son of Rav Ika:
This is what the baraita teaches:
We do not value a kav by itself,
because that gives the injured party an advantage;
and not a kav within a beit kor,
phrases.notes: The small damaged spot is priced as just a tiny piece of a huge field, so it looks worth almost nothing.

phrases.english: because that puts the injured party at a disadvantage;
rather, we value it as one part of sixty.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא, הָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב פפא's rejected reading with a new reading that fits the word 'בית כור'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reading of the ברייתא (הכי קתני)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא spoke of a כור valued as part of sixty כורין, as רב פפא said, which does not fit the word 'בית'.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both clauses are about a damaged קב. It is not valued alone and not within a בית כור, but as one part of sixty.

steps.title: The cut-down date palm and the ריש גלותא's ruling
steps.stepSummary: A man cut down his friend's date palm. The ריש גלותא ruled he must pay a third of the cluster's value, and the man rejected the ruling as Persian law.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man cut down a date palm belonging to his friend. He came before the ריש גלותא, who said to him: I saw it myself. Three palms were standing together in one cluster, and they were worth a hundred זוז. Go give him thirty-three and a third. The man said: Why do I need the ריש גלותא, who judges by Persian law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case that will test the 'one part of sixty' rule. This sets up רב נחמן's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ריש גלותא simply charged a full third of the cluster's value, since one of three trees was cut. He did not use the sixty rule at all. The man felt this was not the law of the תורה and went to a different judge.

keyTerms.meaning: The Exilarch, the official head of the Jews in Babylonia
Persian law, not the law of the תורה

phrases.english: There was a certain man who cut down a date palm belonging to his friend.
He came before the Exilarch.
The Exilarch said to him: I myself saw it,
and three date palms were standing in one cluster,
phrases.notes: 'קינא' literally means a nest. Here it means the palms grew close together as one group.

phrases.english: and they were worth a hundred zuz.

phrases.aramaic: זִיל הַב לֵיהּ תְּלָתִין וּתְלָתָא וְתִילְתָּא.
phrases.english: Go give him thirty-three and a third.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: גַּבֵּי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא דְּדָאֵין דִּינָא דְּפָרְסָאָה, לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: The man said: Why do I need the Exilarch, who judges by Persian law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the ברייתא to a real court case about valuing damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ריש גלותא charged one third of the full value of the three-palm cluster, without using the sixty rule.

steps.title: רב נחמן rules: one part of sixty
steps.stepSummary: The man brought the case to רב נחמן, who ruled the tree is valued as one part of sixty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רב נחמן. רב נחמן said to him: The damage is valued as one part of sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rules on the same case and applies the sixty rule we have been learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of charging a full third, רב נחמן values the cut tree as part of an area sixty times larger. This gives a much smaller payment than the ריש גלותא's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading Babylonian אמורא and judge
He came before him for judgment

phrases.english: He came before Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman said to him: As one part of sixty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different ruling on the case brought in Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cut date palm is valued as one part of sixty.

steps.title: רבא: the sixty rule was for damage by property, not by one's own body
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב נחמן: the sixty rule was taught for damage done by one's property, so why apply it to damage done by a person himself?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If the חכמים said this rule for damage caused by a person's property, would they say it for damage caused by his own body?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רב נחמן's ruling from the step before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sixty rule came up for an animal eating in a field, which is damage by one's property. Here the man cut the tree down himself, which is damage by his own body. רבא argues that a person who damages with his own hands should not get the easier sixty valuation.

keyTerms.meaning: A major Babylonian אמורא, student of רב נחמן
Damage caused by one's property, such as his animal
Damage a person causes with his own body

steps.whyThisMatters: It raises the idea that the sixty rule may not apply to every kind of damage. It may depend on whether the damage was done by one's property or by one's own body.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If they said this about damage caused by his property,
would they say it about damage caused by his own body?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: אִם אָמְרוּ בְּנִזְקֵי מָמוֹנוֹ, יֹאמְרוּ בְּנִזְקֵי גוּפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's ruling in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's use of the sixty rule for a man who cut down a tree himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The sixty rule was given for damage by one's property. Damage by one's own body is more serious, so it should not get the same lenient valuation.

steps.title: אביי asks רבא for the source of his distinction
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבא why he thinks the sixty rule does not apply to damage done by a person's own body. He suggests רבא's source is a ברייתא about ruining a vineyard that mentions only 'before and after' valuing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: When a person causes damage with his own body, what is your reasoning? Is it because of the ברייתא that says: if someone ruins his friend's vineyard while the grapes are just budding, we check how much it was worth before and how much it is worth after? Is it because that ברייתא does not mention the sixty rule?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is asking רבא where his idea comes from, and he guesses the source himself. This sets up אביי's next move, where he will push back on that source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said in step 19 that the sixty rule is only for damage done by one's property. אביי suggests the reason: a ברייתא about a person who ruins a vineyard values the damage only by 'before and after' and says nothing about sixty. רבא would read that silence as proof that the sixty rule does not apply to a person.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage a person does with his own body
One who ruins the young fruit (here, of a vineyard)
The budding stage of grapes, right after the flowers fall
We check how much it was worth (the 'before and after' valuing)

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rava:
Regarding damage done by one's own body, what is your reasoning?
Is it because it was taught in a ברייתא:
One who ruins his friend's vineyard while the grapes are budding –

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתוֹ כַּמָּה הָיָה יָפֶה קוֹדֶם לָכֵן,
phrases.english: we look at how much it was worth before,
and how much it is worth afterward;
whereas 'in sixty' it does not teach?
phrases.notes: This is the 'one part of sixty' way of valuing that רב נחמן used back in step 18.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרָבָא: בְּנִזְקֵי גוּפוֹ מַאי דַּעְתָּיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי responds to רבא's challenge (step 19) by asking for, and guessing at, its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is רבא's basis for saying the sixty rule does not apply to damage done by a person's own body?

steps.title: אביי shows an animal-damage ברייתא also leaves out the sixty rule
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects the proof. A ברייתא about damage by an animal also values the damage without mentioning sixty, yet everyone agrees the sixty rule applies to animals. So the vineyard ברייתא's silence proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that for damage by one's animal there is no similar teaching? There is! It was taught: if an animal broke down a young tree, רבי יוסי says the decree-makers of Jerusalem ruled: a one-year-old tree is worth two silver coins, a two-year-old tree four silver coins. If an animal ate young green grain, רבי יוסי הגלילי says: it is judged by what is left of the field. The חכמים say: we check how much the field was worth before and how much it is worth now.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי knocks down the source he just suggested for רבא. He shows that even for animal damage, where the sixty rule surely applies, a ברייתא gives 'before and after' valuing without mentioning sixty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If silence about sixty proved that the sixty rule does not apply, then this animal ברייתא would prove the rule does not apply to animals either. That cannot be right, because the sixty rule was taught for animal damage. So the vineyard ברייתא may simply not be spelling everything out, and it is no proof for רבא's distinction.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a pushback)
It (an animal) broke down a young tree
The judges in Jerusalem who set fixed rulings
Judged by what remains of it

steps.whatToRemember: Just because a ברייתא does not mention the sixty rule does not mean the rule does not apply. אביי proves this with an animal case, where the sixty rule definitely applies, yet it is also not mentioned.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying the vineyard ברייתא uses the sixty rule. He only says its silence is no proof against it.

phrases.english: Is that to say that regarding his animal too

phrases.aramaic: מִי לָא תַּנְיָא כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא?!
phrases.english: it was not taught in this same way?!
For it was taught: if it broke down a young tree –
phrases.notes: The 'it' is an animal, which is why this proves something about animal damage.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says,
the decree-makers of Jerusalem say:
a young tree in its first year – two silver coins,
two years old – four silver coins.
If it ate young green grain –

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי אוֹמֵר: נִידּוֹן בַּמְשׁוּיָּיר שֶׁבּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says: it is judged by what remains of it,
and the Sages say:
we look at how much it was worth,
and how much it is worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ גַּבֵּי בְהֶמְתּוֹ נָמֵי מִי לָא תַּנְיָא כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof suggested in step 20 by showing that the same silence appears in an animal-damage ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the vineyard ברייתא as a source for רבא's distinction between damage by a person and damage by property.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Arguing from silence fails: an animal-damage ברייתא also omits the sixty rule, even though the sixty rule applies to animals.
